newsitem.title: HAITI: Haiti polls -- success or "lost opportunity"?.
newsitem.headline: Haiti polls -- success or "lost opportunity"?.

text.p: The Haitian government on Monday called senate and local elections a success despite a low voter turnout.
But a foreign observer group called Sunday's polls a "lost opportunity" that showed both how shallow democracy is in this impoverished country and how disillusioned people are with politicians.

Top government officials were determinedly upbeat on Monday, saying the voting went smoothly in most parts of the country -- the poorest in the Western Hemisphere. "The elections were completed with little incident," President Rene Preval told Reuters outside the National Palace on Monday.

Prime Minister Rosny Smarth characterised the vote, in which nine seats in the 27-seat Senate, two parliamentary seats and nearly 700 local positions were up for grabs, as a huge undertaking that went off largely as planned.
"The important thing is that we provided the logistics, financing and security for the population to vote," he said.

Neither cared to comment in depth on what appeared to be a de facto boycott by voters frustrated by continued hardship and poverty despite the ouster of the former military regime. Although more than four million Haitians were registered, only handfuls turned up at many polling stations to vote.
"It isn't up to me to guess why some people didn't participate," Preval said.
Secretary of State for Security Robert Manuel said security would be stepped up for candidates pending final results as some candidates and election officials had been threatened.
"This election has been a success for the Haitian National Police although we must remain vigilant to ensure the vote is not marred by violence," he said.

One death was reported. Celouinord Cheri, an observer for the Open Door Party, part of the ruling Lavalas coalition, was killed on Sunday by unidentified gunmen who shot him twice in the head near Port-au-Prince as he returned home, the party said.

The low turnout seemed from early counts to have helped the Fanmi Lavalas, set up by former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to oppose policies of the Lavalas Political Organisation that originally swept him to power in 1990.
Fanmi Lavalas opposes Preval's programme to privatise state services, a plan backed by international donors but which has angered Haiti's poor.

In the southern city of Jacmel, Fanmi Lavalas candidate Forel Celestain, running with visible support from Aristide, read from exit poll lists on Sunday night indicating a landslide. "More people would have voted," Celestain said. "But the population is discouraged with the process we are trying to change."
Another Fanmi Lavalas candidate, Yvon Neptune, made a horn-honking victory sweep of the capital on Sunday night although official results are not expected until April 28.

Despite the government's positive assessment of the poll, a U.S. observer team said it was a "lost opportunity" that set back efforts to make democracy take root in Haiti. The low turnout indicated frustration and disillusionment among the electorate, Utah Lt. Gov. Olene Walker, leader of the International Republican Institute delegation, told a news briefing on Monday.

"Such sentiments, which appear to be widespread, are not encouraging for Haiti's democratic development," Walker said. "The weak turnout severely undermines the process begun in 1990 and now places an even greater responsibility on Haiti's government and all the nation's leaders to overcome yesterday's lost opportunity."
